title: The sequential replicant effect in interpersonal sincerity: evidence from AI-mediated apology and gratitude
authors: Bolin Cao, Zhenming Li
abstract: Sincerity, a core interpersonal value that mobilizes emotional resources, faces distinct challenges in AI-mediated interpersonal contexts. Extending the Replicant Effect from informational trust to interpersonal sincerity, this study examines how AIMC awareness and AI involvement cues shape sincerity judgments and subsequent relational responses. Drawing on two pre-registered, two-round studies in apology (N = 546) and gratitude (N = 561) scenarios, we found that AI involvement cues reliably reduced perceived sincerity. Primed AIMC awareness showed a more sequential influence on later no-cue evaluations through AIMC suspicion. High-ambiguity AI cues produced sequential effects only in the gratitude context. These findings suggest that hybrid human-AI authorship may reshape how interpersonal sincerity is inferred and validated, while also showing that the effects of AI cues and AIMC awareness depend on cue clarity and relational context.

title: Identity and Words: Does Gender-Fair Language Impact Workers’ Gender-Work Identity Integration?
authors: Claudia Manzi, Eleonora Crapolicchio, Valeria Amata Giannella, Maria Giuseppina Pacilli, Gabriele Di Cicco, Verónica Benet-Martínez
abstract: Understanding how individuals integrate their work and non-work identities has become a central concern in research analyzing individual differences in the work context. In particular, gender-work identity integration (GWII) has been proven to significantly impact employee well-being and work adjustment. We present two studies designed to improve GWII by gender-fair language use at work. In Study 1 ( N = 1024), employees of a telecommunication company, after completing a pre-test, received instructions to use either double gender-marking language (DGML, N = 355) or gender-neutral language (GNL, N = 310) in written communication. A third control group ( N = 359) did not receive any instructions. Results show that use of DGML improved employees’ GWII over time, which, in turn, also increased their work engagement and well-being. Study 2 ( N = 219) replicated findings from Study 1 showing that change in DGML use improves GWII, but only under low levels of observed sexist behaviors in the organization. Together, these findings provide evidence of the impact of organizational language policies on employees’ identity processes and well-being.
journal_full: Journal of Language and Social Psychology

title: ChangeMyView: Unpacking the Complex Emotional, Cognitive, and Communicator-Related Processes Underlying Persuasion
authors: Isabella M. Swafford, Alfonso Carballo, Ryan L. Boyd, Vanessa Kountakis, Lucy McGregor, Vivian P. Ta-Johnson
abstract: Persuasion is shaped by complex emotional triggers, cognitive reasoning, and communicator-related characteristics. However, theories of persuasion have often examined different features of persuasive communication in controlled research settings, resulting in questions about how these characteristics exist within naturally occurring persuasive messages. This study addresses this gap by examining theoretically relevant linguistic characteristics associated with successful persuasion using r/ChangeMyView , an online debate forum where users attempt to change others’ views on any topic, and posts resulting in successful persuasion are marked. In Study 1, Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count was used to analyze n = 9020 r/ChangeMyView posts from 2013 to 2018. Principal component analyses identified three broad linguistic dimensions reflecting cognitive reasoning, emotional expression, and authentic communication style. These components were then entered into a multilevel logistic regression analysis, revealing that greater scores on the cognitive reasoning dimension were associated with lower persuasive likelihood, whereas emotional expression and authentic communication were not significantly associated with persuasion. Study 2 analyzed 51,394 posts from 2019 to 2023 and identified a similar three-component structure, demonstrating consistency in how the selected linguistic characteristics grouped across samples. Cognitive reasoning again predicted lower persuasive likelihood, while greater emotional expression predicted lower persuasive likelihood and authentic communication predicted greater persuasive likelihood. The results suggest that naturally occurring persuasive language organizes into reproducible but nuanced dimensions, and that multiple forms of linguistic information contribute to persuasive messaging. Overall, the findings provide naturalistic evidence relevant to theoretical accounts that conceptualize persuasion as involving multiple, potentially overlapping forms of information processing.

title: Methods Hub: A Community-Driven, Interactive Platform for Open-Source Computational Tools and Tutorials
authors: Christina Viehmann, Johannes Kiesel, Arnim Bleier, Chung-hong Chan, Po-Chun Chang, Raniere Gaia Costa da Silva, Ahrabhi Kathirgamalingam, Taimoor Khan, Stephan Linzbach, Fakhri Momeni, Felix Münch, Ran Yu, Stefan Dietze, Claudia Wagner
abstract: As computational methods become increasingly central to social science research, there is a growing demand for research software infrastructures that are sustainable, grounded in principles of open science, and embedded in the community. In response, we are introducing the Methods Hub as an open-source, community-driven collection of computational tools designed to support social science research in solving complex data-related tasks. The Methods Hub integrates three complementary components: First, quality-curated content, including computational methods and accompanying tutorials, which are specifically presented from a social science research perspective. Second, the methods and tutorials are hosted on a web portal enabling researchers to discover, apply, learn, and publish computational methods. Third, interactive, browser-based execution backends allow users to directly run, test, and adapt the code of methods and tutorials. These components are guided by a set of core principles: a long-term infrastructure perspective, reproducibility requirements, and a focus on community. The Methods Hub builds a long-term infrastructure that extends beyond the scope of single projects. Further, reproducibility functions as a quality assurance measure while advancing the practices of open science. Finally, the Methods Hub is built on public, community-based submissions by treating research software as citable academic output and providing visibility, accessibility, and formal recognition. We are also broadening the community by fostering learning and ease of access. Looking ahead, the Methods Hub is exploring the potential of AI as both a research tool and to further strengthen the infrastructure, while maintaining transparency, reproducibility, and quality standards for computational social science research.

title: Social Media “Image Operations” During the Tigray War (2020–2022)
authors: Matti Pohjonen, Amanuel Tesfaye Kebede
abstract: This article examines the use of social media images during the Tigray War (2020–2022), one of the world’s deadliest armed conflicts of the 21st century. Drawing on a corpus of 92.9 million tweets and over 500,000 images shared on Twitter, we analyse what types of images were shared by the opposing sides of the conflict and what specific functions these images served in antagonistic information campaigns. The article shows how images were used not only to amplify the opposing strategic narratives about war but also to shape the emotional or affective registers related to it. The pro-Tigray campaign relied on the heavy use of emotive images of casualties as well as images of material destruction, which, combined with the use of infographics, collectively conveyed victimhood with the goal of putting pressure on the Ethiopian government and its allies. The pro-government side, in turn, relied more on images that tried to evoke patriotism and resistance in the audience, organise protests, as well as represent a stance of anti-colonial defiance against international pressure. The article contributes to the growing literature on digital media in contemporary conflicts by proposing a novel research framework and methodology and providing original empirical findings on an understudied dimension of contemporary conflicts.

title: Why research on science communication needs more meta-analyses
authors: Niels G. Mede, Mike S. Schäfer, Elisa Tedaldi
abstract: Research on science communication has expanded and diversified. Correspondingly, an increasing number of literature reviews, handbooks, and bibliometric studies have taken stock of the field’s accumulated knowledge. However, it is still difficult to identify robust, consolidated answers to key questions on science communication—answers that may help scholars, practitioners, and decision-makers. Meta-analyses—the statistical aggregation of empirical results across multiple studies to determine average effect sizes—can provide some of those answers, complementing existing knowledge syntheses and addressing their shortcomings. Yet, meta-analyses in research on science communication are rare, whereas other disciplines are much closer to establishing a culture of meta-analyses and demonstrate the usefulness of meta-analyses for specific aspects of science communication research within and beyond our discipline. We therefore propose a meta-analytical research agenda of science communication scholarship and argue that it will increase the impact of our field in the social sciences and society.

title: Seeing Is Believing? Most People Struggle to Detect AI-Generated Images
authors: Mads Fuglsang Hove, Frederik Hjorth, Yevgeniy Golovchenko, Rebecca Adler-Nissen, Anja Bechmann, Arjen van Dalen, Sara B. Hobolt, Claes de Vreese
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) dramatically lowers the costs of creating high-quality, realistic images, allowing a wider range of actors to create and distribute such content on, for instance, social media. A core concern is that easy-to-use generative AI tools can be misused for manipulation through misinformation and microtargeted persuasive material. However, we still need more contextual nuance to a fundamental question: To what degree can people discern photorealistic AI-generated images from authentic images? In a preregistered survey experiment, we find that, on average, people are not substantially better than chance at discerning AI-generated images from authentic images, regardless of the context of the image. While younger people, highly analytical-thinking individuals, and experienced users of generative AI have better discernment abilities, no demographic group other than young individuals (<25) performs substantially better than chance. Contrary to our expectation, we do not find that people’s confidence in their discernment abilities varies depending on the context of the image. As generative AI technology likely advances and the realism of AI-generated images continues to improve, these findings are concerning, as people already struggle to discern between AI-generated and authentic images, even in an experiment where they have been primed and are assessing images of relatively low quality.

title: Television Time and Electoral Success: Evidence From the Constitutional Convention Election in Chile in 2021
authors: Roberto Munita-Morgan, Patricio Navia
abstract: Some democracies give all political parties free television time to level the electoral campaign playing field. Relying on a case that uses open-list proportional representation rules and where voters select individual candidates, but where free television time is assigned to party lists, we explore the association between appearing in free television ads (franja) and electoral success in Chile’s 2021 Constitutional Convention election. In this unprecedented contest, airtime was allocated to parties and lists of independents. We use an original coding of 3,157 mentions across 28 days of television ads for candidates in the four largest electoral lists (692 candidates). Candidates mentioned in ads received higher vote shares (2.9 vs. 2.2 percent) and were more likely to win seats (18.6 vs. 7.7 percent). Multivariate models show that campaign spending is more strongly associated with electoral success, but mentions in the franja have a modest but statistically significant positive coefficient. Although we cannot disentangle the potential endogeneity of being more electable and appearing in the franja, the findings highlight the importance of television time for electoral success and point to how party-controlled media exposure influences intra-list competition.

title: Strategic alienation: The dynamics of group appeals in negative campaigning
authors: Lena Maria Huber, Martin Haselmayer
abstract: This paper examines how political parties use social group appeals in negative campaigning. We argue that parties strategically target opponents with group-based attacks to portray them as failing key social groups. Using a novel dataset of Facebook and Twitter posts by parties in the UK (2016–2024), linked to voter perceptions of group representation from the British Election Study, we test whether such attacks are more likely when the sender party enjoys strong group-based credibility, or the target party is seen as a weak representative of the respective group, or both. We find no evidence for the former but strong support for the latter: parties disproportionately target rivals with poor reputations for representing specific groups, and especially so when the sender holds a reputational advantage. These findings advance our understanding of identity-driven party competition, showing that group-based attacks exploit opponents’ representational vulnerabilities rather than reinforce attackers’ own strength.

title: Powered by (discrete) emotions? The consequences of affective polarization for self-censorship and outgroup silencing
authors: Luna Laufer, Laura Gerstner, Pia Kinzler, Julia Stockwald, Anna-Luisa Sacher, Carsten Reinemann
abstract: Amid ongoing debates about political polarization in Western Democracies, this study investigates the role of affective polarization in the context of practices related to political discourse. In doing so, it moves beyond generalized affective polarization and delves into discrete negative emotions (fear, disgust, and anger), examining how they relate to the willingness to engage in self-censorship and the belief in the importance of silencing others, i.e., the respective political outgroup. Findings from a quota-based online survey conducted in autumn 2024 in Germany ( N = 1,918) reveal that the effects of affective polarization vary depending on the underlying emotion: fear of the political outgroup is linked to an increased willingness to self-censor. In contrast, anger is associated with a reduced willingness to self-censor, while all three negative emotions are connected to a higher belief in the importance to silence the political outgroup. These results underscore the critical role of discrete emotions in affective polarization, offering nuanced insights that extend beyond generalized dislike. In addition, they provide valuable insights into how affective polarization may threaten democratic values.

title: What Works Against Populist Rhetoric? The Effects of Counter-Arguments on Democratic Attitudes
authors: Markus Kollberg, Julia Leschke
abstract: Politicians use populist rhetoric – arguments that portray politics as an enduring conflict between “the good people” and “the evil elites” – to generate support for attacks on constitutional safeguards, the media, and minorities. Yet, little is known about how to counteract such rhetoric. We utilize a pre-registered survey experiment in the UK (n $$\cong$$ 4000) to investigate the effects of counter-arguments put forward by fellow citizens. We hypothesize pluralist and democratic elitist counter-arguments to be promising antidotes to populist rhetoric and test to what extent such arguments can strengthen liberal democratic attitudes and weaken populist majoritarian ones. We find that populism can be challenged successfully but not with all types of counter-arguments. Pluralist appeals can decrease support for populist majoritarian democracy, while elitist counter-arguments have no effect on democratic attitudes. Additional analyses suggest that counter-arguments might also affect how voters evaluate candidates. These results contribute by demonstrating the potentials of counter-arguments in strengthening the resilience of liberal democracies vis-à-vis populist challenges.

title: Bad news for (young) gamers: Using gaming platforms as news sources is more intimately associated with radical belief dispositions than other online spaces
authors: Simon Greipl, Ulrike Schwertberger, Diana Rieger, Brigitte Naderer
abstract: This study explores how digital news use among young Europeans links to radical belief dispositions, particularly within gaming platforms and messengers, where socio‐affective dynamics shape engagement with political information. We argue that online groups are an overlooked locus for biased information processing and the normalization of extremist worldviews. The conflation of an increasingly fragmented online news space with the inherently politicized gaming cosmos can relate to amplified problematic worldviews based on shared activity, identity, and reality. Based on a cross‐country survey ( N = 1489; eight European countries), we compare (the use of) gaming, messenger apps, social media, and traditional media for news in terms of how they afford problematic forms of collectivity, particularly in relation to social, cynical, and radical epistemologies. We find a robust correlation between news use and a set of radical belief dispositions, prominently with messenger apps, but even more so in gaming‐related online environments—less so on social media and none with traditional news use. Notably, a mediation analysis suggests that shared meaning‐making exhibits a negative rather than a positive indirect association with radical belief dispositions. We discuss the complex interplay of how individual factors and platform architectures connect with news engagement utilizing a vulnerability‐affordance framework.

title: Understanding when mixture models effectively identify careless responding: Simulation and validity evidence
authors: Irina Uglanova, Gabriel Nagy, Esther Ulitzsch
abstract: Careless and insufficient effort responding (C/IER) in self-report questionnaires refers to responses provided without adequate attention to item content. Latent variable mixture models have recently been proposed as a promising approach for detecting and accounting for C/IER. This study systematically evaluates the performance of mixture modeling for C/IER detection. Using an exemplar mixture model that captures core features of existing approaches, we (a) investigated, via simulations, conditions that facilitate or impede separation between response patterns indicative of attentive versus careless responding and (b) examined the validity of interpreting the latent class variable as an indicator of C/IER in an empirical application. The simulation study assessed how questionnaire and item characteristics affect latent-class identification under different C/IER response patterns. Results indicate that reliable separation is achieved when scales comprise at least ten items, exhibit substantial threshold heterogeneity, and include both positively and negatively worded items. Empirical support for the C/IER interpretation of the latent class variable was obtained by reanalyzing a publicly available Big Five inventory data set collected across multiple platforms. Model-based classifications closely corresponded to alternative C/IER indicators that do not rely on response patterns, exhibited consistency across multiple scales, and were sensitive to platform-specific differences in C/IER prevalence. Overall, the results support mixture modeling as a viable approach for addressing C/IER under many conditions commonly encountered in applied research.

title: Algorithm-assisted personalized risk communication to encourage flu vaccination in the USA: three randomized field trials
authors: Gail M. Rosenbaum, Amir Goren, Maheen Shermohammed, Donna M. Wolk, Ann Marie Tice, Joseph J. Doyle, Michelle N. Meyer, Christopher F. Chabris
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in healthcare to identify high-risk patients. Laboratory studies are mixed regarding patient attitudes towards AI use. Here we field-tested whether informing patients of their risk for influenza and its complications can serve as an effective behaviour-change intervention to increase vaccination, and whether disclosing AI use in the risk determination or providing personalized reasons for the algorithm’s prediction (a form of explainable AI) influence message effectiveness. We ran three preregistered randomized controlled trials with over 90,000 unique healthcare system patients in the USA (ClinicalTrials.gov identifiers: NCT04323137, NCT05009251 and NCT05509283). Patients identified by a previously validated machine learning algorithm as being at high risk for influenza and related complications were randomized to be sent no message or one of several different messages encouraging influenza vaccination (the primary outcome). High-risk nudges increased vaccination: among patients informed of their high risk, vaccination was 1.1–1.4 percentage points (3.3–5.4%) higher than those simply reminded to get a vaccine, and 1.7–3.5 percentage points (3.3–14.7%) higher than non-messaged patients. Vaccination was similar across message arms that did versus did not disclose ‘algorithm’ involvement or its risk explanations, indicating that patients are neither averse to nor appreciative of algorithm use or explainability in this realistic health application. This work was partially funded by the National Institute on Aging of the National Institutes of Health under award number P30AG034532.
